image_description:
## 1. Chart type
A **two-panel horizontal bar chart**:
- **Left panel:** horizontal bar chart of greenhouse gas impact by protein source
- **Right panel:** horizontal bar chart of consumer food waste/loss percentage by food category

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Side-by-side panels** showing two separate bar charts
- No faceting grid, no stacking, and no small multiples within each panel
- Bars are **sorted** within each panel by value

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Protein source (Beef, Lamb, Farmed crustaceans, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Average greenhouse gas impact (kg CO₂ for 50g protein) | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis; numeric labels on bars |
| Food category (Fish and seafood, Fresh fruit, etc.) | Categorical/nominal | Position on y-axis; text labels |
| Percentage of food wasted or lost at consumer level | Quantitative | Bar length / position on x-axis; percentage labels on bars |
| Panel/topic (greenhouse gas impact vs food waste/loss) | Categorical/nominal | Spatial separation into left and right panels; titles |

This graph displays the degree of human impact on the planet and how our choices can determine the fate of the climate.  It compares various food sources and their carbon dioxide output.  Greenhouse gases can be ozone-depleting and can force change in the climate.  The left side of the graph shows how many kilograms of carbon dioxide is being emitted as we eat protein-rich food items.  
The opposite side of the graph depicts food waste and which types of food create the most waste.  Food waste begins to rot and becomes a significant source of methane, another prevalent greenhouse gas pollutant.  The overarching effect of the graph is an awareness of how easily we can reduce our negative effects on the planet.

comments.raw_comment: This graph is depicting how much different foods people eat impact greenhouse gasses. Beef is the biggest 17.7kg of CO2 per 50 grams. That's pretty insane. The average hamburger is around 113 grams. That means for every hamburger there is approximately 35.4kg of CO2 emitted into the atmosphere.  Now on the other side of the picture we have a different graph showing how much people waste certain types of food. The most waste comes from seafood and fish. I would assume that’s because seafood spoils relatively fast. If people were willing to prepare a serving of fish (which is typically around 140 grams) you would be emitting around 9kg CO2. This means that one hamburger would emit the same amount of CO2 as almost FOUR servings of fish. Fish is clearly the better choice when it comes to greenhouse gasses.

comments.raw_comment: This graph is showing the percentage of food that is wasted and the average greenhouse gas impact. I noticed that beef has the biggest greenhouse gas impact with 17.7. I noticed that the foods that are highly perishable, such as fish, veggies, and fruit, are the most commonly wasted, and foods that are not perishable, such as grains, are at the bottom of the graph.

comments.raw_comment:
When I looked at the graph on the left I first noticed how damaging raising cattle is to the environment.  Getting 50 grams of protein from beef causes the release of 17.7 kilograms of Carbon Dioxide into the environment.  This is almost twice the Carbon Dioxide that is produced when the same amount of protein is extracted from lambs.  According to the graph, lamb and beef account for just under half of the total amount of Carbon Dioxide produced by farming crustaceans, cheese, pork, farmed fish, poultry, eggs, tofu, beans, and nuts combined.  

The graph proves how certain diets such as veganism, pescetarianism and vegetarianism help minimize the destruction of the environment by limiting the production of greenhouse gases.  These diets promote sustainable consumption and use of animals and animal products.  Veganism is the most extreme of these three diets because followers limit themselves to absolutely no consumption of animals or their byproducts.  On the graph, a vegan would only eat tofu, beans and nuts which combine to just 1.5 kilograms of greenhouse gas produced from getting 50 grams of protein from each of the three foods.  This is just 8% of the greenhouse gases produced from 50 grams of protein from beef.  If we want to decrease our negative impact on the environment a great way to start is by decreasing our consumption of beef and mammals in general.

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded.  We had so many great catchy headlines that capture the main ideas of the graphs:  "Doomed by Food" by Sage of Tumwater, Washington, "Cut Out Meat, Veggies to Eat! (Don’t Waste It!)" by Mrs. Lane ELP class at North Star Elementary School in Salt Lake City, Utah, “"Mother Nature Has Beef with Beef." by Sophie, Mady, Keegan, Lauren of Eden Prairie, Minnesota, and “Eating Away the Earth” by Lauren of Academy of Saint Elizabeth, in Morristown, New Jersey.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back tomorrow --  Thursday afternoon, December 12 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graphs, and a few Stat Nuggets.
The next graph will be released tomorrow – Thursday, January 2, with moderation on Wednesday, January 8.  You may respond before, during, or after the live moderation by going to ““What's Going On In This Graph?”  The topic --  internet privacy policies.  

You can see all of the released graphs on the “What’s Going On In This Graph?” homepage.  Or, go to our post “Looking for Graphs to Use in the Classroom? Here Are 34.” for an index by context and an index by type of graph. The link for the Stat Nuggets archives ishttps://tinyurl.com/StatNuggets.

Signing off – Sharon Hessney of Boston, who should reduce her food carbon footprint, and Leigh Nataro of Moravian College, Easton, Pennsylvania, who loves vegan desserts despite their high sugar content.

comments.raw_comment: I believe that this graph is demonstrating how detrimental our waste can be. The two highest CO2 producing industries are beef and lamb, at 17.7 kg and 9.9 kg respectively. It just so happens that meat and poultry is the third most wasted commodity, at 21% wasted. This means that of that 17.7 kg it took to make just 50 g of protein, 3.717 kg are completely wasted. This may seem minimal when you look at just one 50 g portion of beef, but when you do the math, it really adds up. In 2016, the world consumed about 129.5 billion pounds of beef, and each pound is 117g of protein. When you multiply this and divide it by 50g (to get the amount of times 17.7 kg carbon is produced), and proceed to multiply that by 17.7 kg, it gives you the final answer of total kilograms of CO2 produced because of beef worldwide, and multiplying that by .21 gives the total amount wasted. And that answer is: 1.13 trillion kg of CO2 wasted from beef every year - and that's only beef! I wonder why the graphs are side by side, as these two graphs help Americans reduce their cognitive dissonance as they make unsustainable decisions about what to eat. We're all aware that we should cut meat out of our diet for the sake of the environment. However, when I see that I'm more likely to waste fruits and vegetables, I could justify my choice to not cut out meat by saying that buying alternatives for my diet would lead to more wastage, which is environmentally bad due to deadweight loss. 

The two issues can be solved by changing the unit of the bar graph to the left. Instead of kilograms of carbon dioxide per 50 grams of protein, it should be equivalent kilograms of carbon dioxide per pound of food. Doing equivalent kilograms of carbon dioxide ensures that other emissions, such as methane, are accounted for. Just convert the damage done per gram of emitted methane to emitted gram of carbon dioxide. Listing the emissions per pound of food allows Americans to conceptualize just how harmful some of their dietary choices are for the environment. Additionally, doing quantity of food, as opposed to quantity of protein, means that Americans can also see just how efficient fruits and vegetables (in general, not niche products like beans and nuts) are to meat, so they have a harder time justifying their choices compared to the current graph.

comments.raw_comment:
Many Americans have an unrealistic idea that our waste just disappears when the trash people come pick it up and our food has no impact on our Earth. I saw a graph similar to this one in 2017 and it changed the way I viewed our food consumption and waste system in the United States. Environmental consciousness is important to me, so after doing some research, I decided to try to cut back on beef products. 

The graph shows the GHG emissions associated with certain foods that provide protein. Beans and nuts are at the bottom (least emissions), and beef and lamb at the top (most emissions). The graph reinforces the idea that plant based diets are more environmentally friendly than those including animal products. Within the last year, I have gradually gone completely vegan solely because of the environmental impacts of meat and animal products, as shown in the graph. 

However, I often have doubts about the true impact I’m having with the diet. Just 10-20% of green house gas emissions actually come from agriculture/animal food industry, the rest from electricity/transportation/industry sources. So, even if every person on the planet went vegan, there would still be 80-90% of the original amount of fossil fuels being added to our atmosphere. 

This graph brings up an incredibly controversial, yet important topic with many viewpoints. I’m curious to eventually read other student’s comments.
